findings.description: AWS access key and secret access key are hard-coded in plaintext in the EC2 user_data script, exposing long-lived IAM credentials to anyone with access to instance metadata, console, or Terraform state.
Ingress rule allows SSH (port 22) from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing the management port to the entire internet and enabling brute-force or credential-stuffing attacks.
Ingress rule allows HTTP (port 80) from 0.0.0.0/0 with no compensating controls (e.g., WAF, TLS), exposing the web service broadly and only over cleartext HTTP.
Egress rule allows all outbound traffic to 0.0.0.0/0 on all ports/protocols, increasing risk of data exfiltration if the instance is compromised.

Subnet auto-assigns public IPs to launched instances (map_public_ip_on_launch = true), increasing the exposure surface for any resources placed here, including the EC2 instance with an open SSH ingress rule.
Subnet auto-assigns public IPs to launched instances (map_public_ip_on_launch = true), widening the network's public attack surface unnecessarily.
The EBS volume does not set encrypted = true, so data stored on the volume (and any snapshots taken from it) is stored unencrypted at rest.
The snapshot is taken from an unencrypted EBS volume and inherits the lack of encryption, exposing data at rest if the snapshot is shared or exfiltrated.

The S3 bucket storing VPC flow logs has no server-side encryption configuration (aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration), leaving potentially sensitive network traffic metadata unencrypted at rest.

findings.issue_category: missing access controls / public access block
findings.description: No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block or bucket policy is defined to explicitly deny public access, and force_destroy is enabled, increasing risk of accidental public exposure or data loss of flow log archives.
